first.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing is the loudest signal, but the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and memory_73 explicitly records that promotional pricing bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and carries an explicit do-not-generalize caveat. Matching the competitor on price would trade the exact quantity I am asked to maximize. The two things actually degrading (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are internal and are the ones I can move.

Between the two internal fits: memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifting completion and time-to-value) sits upstream of both declining metrics, while memory_91 (activation messaging) addresses only one. memory_31 corroborates the signup-friction direction independently, which is why I lean to simplify_onboarding. I am spending my two pulls on memory_86 (the record I intend to act on, to see actual effect size, cohort, and whether the lift persisted past the measurement window) and memory_91 (the strongest alternative and the most recent record, to check whether its activation lift was large enough to prefer the narrower intervention).

Downstream value risk: friction removal is not value-neutral. memory_31's mechanism was cutting required signup fields, and required fields often double as qualification and routing signal. Reducing them can raise raw activation while lowering the share of accounts that become qualified revenue, and can misroute enterprise prospects away from the sales-assisted path that memory_44 says converts better. So I will hold the enterprise demo-request route untouched, keep any field cuts to non-qualifying fields, and instrument on qualified-pipeline and 30-day retention rather than completion or activation alone. Otherwise I risk reproducing the promotional-pricing failure mode with a different lever: a clean short-horizon metric masking value erosion.

Uncertainty I am not collapsing: these are consolidated summaries, not results. Effect sizes, sample sizes, segments, and durability are absent, and memory_86 and memory_31 are 15 and 64 days old against a competitive environment that changed this quarter. A prior lift on a healthy baseline may not replicate on a declining one, and the current decline may have a cause (traffic mix shifting toward price-shoppers pulled in by the competitor) that no onboarding change can fix. Standard experiment scale with a proper holdout, not a broad rollout: I want a real read, but the inherited evidence is a summary, not a guarantee. If the archive shows memory_86's lift was small, short-lived, or confined to a segment we no longer see, I switch to activation_messaging as the narrower and more recently validated bet.

mid.rationale:
Both records verified as confirmed, and the archive resolves the choice in favor of onboarding. exp_86: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%. exp_91: engagement +11%, activation +6%, retention +1%. Onboarding wins on the metric that actually tracks the objective — retention at +3% versus +1% — and it sits upstream of both declining numbers rather than just one. Shorter time-to-value is also the most direct non-price answer to a competitor's entry pricing: if accounts reach value in two fewer days, the discount matters less. Committing to simplify_onboarding, standard experiment with a holdout.

One thing the archive corrected in my prior reasoning, and it matters. exp_86 was a shortened onboarding flow — fewer steps — not the signup field cuts described in memory_31. Those are different interventions with different risk profiles, and I had partly conflated them. The verified +3% retention belongs to flow shortening only. So I am running flow shortening and explicitly not cutting required signup fields; memory_31 remains an unverified summary and I will not let it smuggle field removal into this test under cover of a result that did not test it.

Downstream value risk still flagged, narrowed to two places. First, shortening a flow can quietly remove qualification and routing steps even when no field is deleted; per memory_44 the enterprise demo-request path outperforms self-serve on pipeline quality, so that route stays untouched and I will check that enterprise-shaped accounts are not being absorbed into the faster self-serve path. Second, exp_86 measured completion, time-to-value and 30-day retention, none of which is qualified revenue. A flow that converts more price-shoppers faster can lift all three while degrading the thing I am asked to maximize. Primary readout is therefore qualified pipeline and 30-day retention by segment; completion is a diagnostic, not the verdict.

Uncertainty preserved. Confirmed does not mean transferable: exp_86 ran on a day-52 baseline, and today's decline may be driven by a traffic-mix shift toward price-sensitive accounts pulled in by the competitor, which no onboarding change repairs. If that is the cause I expect completion to rise while qualified pipeline stays flat, and that pattern should be read as the intervention missing the cause rather than as a partial win. Explicitly rejecting promotional_pricing despite it being the direct competitive counter — memory_73 records real acquisition and revenue lift alongside a material 30-day retention drop and a do-not-generalize caveat, and this quarter's pressure is exactly the condition that caveat was written against. activation_messaging is the verified fallback if this reads flat.

final2.rationale:
Holding simplify_onboarding. The deeper price cut raises urgency but changes no evidence I have, and urgency is precisely the condition memory_73's caveat was written to survive. That record shows promotional pricing buys acquisition and revenue while materially reducing 30-day retention, with an explicit instruction not to generalize it as a growth strategy. Doubled churn conversations with price-sensitive SMB accounts are the exact situation that makes discounting feel forced, and the exact situation where it converts a retention problem into a lower-value book of business. Matching a competitor whose entry pricing we cannot sustain also concedes the pricing frame to the party who chose it.

The verified case stands: exp_86 delivered completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3% — the best retention number I hold, and the only lever that touches both declining metrics. Shorter time-to-value is the substantive non-price answer to a discount: it shrinks the window in which an account is paying without yet having received value, which is when a cheaper competitor is most persuasive. Standard experiment with a holdout, not a broad rollout; a real read is worth more than a fast one, and the panic is not evidence.

I want to be honest about what this decision does not do. It does not save the accounts already in churn conversations this week. Onboarding affects new and early accounts; the at-risk base is mostly past that stage. So my one experiment slot is not a rescue, and I should not present it as one. The correct handling of active churn conversations is retention and account work — pricing exceptions negotiated case by case, which is not the same as a generalized promotional program and does not need this slot. If leadership wants the at-risk base addressed today, that is the honest recommendation, and it is separable from the experiment. referral_incentive (memory_57) is unverified summary and aimed at established customers, wrong instrument for acquisition pressure. enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is also unverified and does not address SMB.

Downstream value risk unchanged and still flagged: shortening the flow must not strip qualification or routing steps, the enterprise demo-request path stays untouched, and I am not cutting signup fields since exp_86 never tested that. Readout remains qualified pipeline and 30-day retention by segment, not completion. Uncertainty preserved: exp_86's lift was measured on a day-52 baseline in a different competitive environment, and if the current decline is a traffic-mix shift toward price-shoppers, completion will rise while qualified pipeline stays flat. That pattern means the intervention missed the cause, not that it partly worked, and next week's archive budget should go to memory_31 and memory_57.
